and that is true in regard to a number of the other favoured nations with which this treaty will help us expand our trade.
But I am delighted with No. 4: "It is the beginning of the destruction of the whole British preferential system for which we have been struggling since 1897." Well, they struggled against it in 1897, so they have not been keeping up a very consistent struggle. The British preference will be able to stand, no matter what may happen. We are not destroying it; we are modifying it. There is a marked difference between destruction and modification. But may I point out that Canada needs the world for a market. It cannot do without it. In 1938 the British empire took approximately 50 per cent of our products, which means that 50 per cent of our products had to be marketed somewhere else. The people of Canada cannot afford to confine their trade to half the nations of the world. They need every market they can get.
Then in No. 5 the hon. gentleman suggests that this cuts into the British market, which he says is our best market for wheat, fruits, lumber and so on. I have grave doubts as to the accuracy of the prophecies of these hon. gentlemen. They were wrong in 1911; they were wrong in 1936, when we brought in the other reciprocity treaty. I recall hearing man after man tell of the ruin that would follow the introduction of the provision permitting duty free imports up to 8100. It was going to wipe out the merchants along the border. But I am not going to deal specifically with these items to-night, because they were dealt with very carefully this afternoon by my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley).
Now I come to No. 6:
It injures our Canadian traffic and damages the transportation system, railways, steamships and so forth, sending traffic north and south instead of east and west.
I want to make this suggestion to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition or to any other Conservative or Liberal in the house. Look at the earnings of the Canadian railways; the report can be found in the Canada Year Book. Look at the imports from the United States. Select to your own satisfaction the four years during which our imports from the United States were largest and the four years when they were lowest in recent years, and I will tell you what you will find. In the four years when our imports were highest our railway earnings were highest, and in the four years when our imports were lowest our railway earnings were lowest. But these boys never learn anything. Of course 
they suggest this is merely a coincidence, but if that coincidence occurs all down through our economic history I wonder what the hon. gentlemen will have to say. If, looking over this house to-night, I noticed a number of gentlemen who had very beautiful heads of hair and knew they were using herpicide, I think I would use herpicide too. I would not think it was a coincidence. But my hon. friends can look at the records of the facts, can stare them in. the face, and the only result is that they intensify their drive in the opposite direction. They think the more emphatically they state their claim that our railways will be ruined by imports, in some way eventually some people 'will come to believe it.
Another argument is that this treaty gives too much in return for too little. Well, what does that amount to? Suppose it increases our trade by 10 per cent and increases the trade of one of the other nations by 25 per cent; we would still be 10 per cent better off than if we accepted the advice of our friends and voted against the treaty. But they seem to have the idea that if it does not benefit all equally it should not be supported. That is a most preposterous suggestion.
Then it is said that we shall lose revenues through the elimination of the 3 per cent excise tax. The 3 per cent excise tax was first applied in 1932. Speaking in this house at the time Mr. Rhodes said:
I have not the slightest hesitation in saying to my right hon. friend that the government is not wedded to it, other than as a necessity of the moment, as a means of taxation.
Later on Mr. Bennett came along, and what did he do? He was not wedded to it at all, because in April 1934, he cut it in half as far as British imports were concerned and in 1935 removed it from those imports .altogether. In those circumstances I wonder if it is not fair to say that if Mr. Bennett had been given the chance, eventually he would have removed it entirely. At least I hope he would have done so, and I am sure he would unless he were persuaded to the contrary by the hon. gentlemen to my left who now hold the view that no tax may be reduced under any circumstances unless they are given the opportunity to do it.
Then my hon. friend said the treaty would probably increase unemployment through greater competition in industries such as coal mining, manufacturing, and so on. Let me say to my hon. friend that time will write that record. In fact, time has already written it. My hon. friends have tried their method of solving the problems of the country, and it has not succeeded. We have succeeded in proving that there is at least some hope for

us when we go in this direction, and we propose to go a good deal further than we have gone as yet.

For the people of
Canada, for the people whom I represent, for the people who want it and know we are going to get it.
That brings me to a very interesting point. Referring to the Americans, my hon. friend said:
Third, they are shrewder traders than we are. I had the word "sharper" in my notes, but I do not like to use it because it might be taken as offensive-
Then he goes on to speak about the down-east Yankee and has this further word to say:
I simply say, Mr. Speaker, that the United States cares for its own people when it is making a trade treaty of this kind.
I want to show how they are taking care of their own people. It is astonishing that in the House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada we should so frequently hear members speak with an attitude of extreme contempt for the Canadian people. Let me show what we have done as far as Canada is concerned. The Economist of December 3, 1938, said that the business recession in Canada was by no means as intense as it was in the United States. The monthly bulletin of the Cleveland Trust Company, written by Leonard Ayers, made practically the same statement. The last issue of the Bank of Nova Scotia bulletin stated that industrial production, factory payrolls, factory employment and revenue carloadings were distinctly higher in Canada than in the United States. That is in relation to the standard index. The only point at which the United States is temporarily ahead of us is in connection with building construction,.where the enormous governmental expenditures of the United States have helped their progress to a certain extent.	*
What happened in regard to trade? Let us consider the index of trade in the two countries. Take 100 as the index number for 1929 in the United States and Canada. In 1932 the United States trade was represented by the figure 31. In Canada in that year, when our Conservative friends were in power, it was represented by an index number 42. In 1938 the United States index number was up to 59, while the Canadian index number 71492-76J
had gone up to 79. I wonder what my hon. friends have to say about that? Are they not proud of their own record back in 1932 when the index number was down to 42, and do they not think they should express at least some appreciation for our efforts when we brought it up to 79?
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition was good enough to tell us that the United States was not a stable market in which to do business, but here again I want to point out that the hon. gentleman was wrong in his conclusion. In our trade with the United Kingdom we moved from an index of 100 in 1926 to 34 in 1932 and up to 80 in 1938. In our trade with the United States we moved from a figure of 100 down to 41 in 1932. We did not go down so far and our recovery was better. In 1938 we had come up to 88. Surely this is a satisfactory indication of the progress we are making so far as trade is concerned.
My hon. friend was good enough the other day to quote from The Economist. I want to quote from the same publication merely to show that it is rather dangerous to quote to this house one part of an article and then forget that in the same article there is a concluding part which alters completely what has been said before. My hon. friend_ made this quotation from The Economist of November, 1926:
It is more questionable whether there will be a corresponding increase in British imports. Very few of the concessions made to the United States will result in any category of American goods being placed in a more favourable competitive position vis-a-vis the domestic producer. Most of the agricultural products affected are not grown in this country, or where they are, the domestic producer is already safeguarded.
My hon. friend quoted that, and he took it to be supreme condemnation of the treaty so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned. But I want to read the concluding paragraph, and then I shall ask my friends if they are going to vote for this treaty, because I do not think they are. I quote:
The immediate effect of the agreement is not to be measured in terms of a diplomatic reinforcement, still less of a strengthening of the military or economic defences, of either of the signatories. But its long-term effects in the purely political field can be negatively assessed by imagining the derisive joy in certain European capitals and the profound depression in others that would have been produced by a failure of the negotiations. To have brought to birth not merely an agreement, but such a good agreement, is a decisive act of economic statesmanship.
I ask hon. gentlemen behind the leader of the opposition what they are going to do when it comes to a vote upon this issue?

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
With utter irresponsibility I know they will certainly vote against it. But I ask them: If you were in power would you vote against it? Would you vote against, it when one of the leading papers, a paper which was quoted by my distinguished friend, tells you that your action would be greeted by derisive joy in certain European capitals and profound depression in others, and that depression would be felt in the nations with which you are affiliated? Oh, yes, it is all right to do it when you think you can do it, and then go out to the people and show what you have done. But it is somewhat different when you face the realities of what it means not only to Canada but to the world. It is a good agreement; it is considered a decisive act of economic statesmanship. Perhaps I should not expect my hon. friends to agree with it.
But I turn to one more item, the famous balance of trade. My distinguished friend, the leader of the opposition, always wants us to have a favourable balance of trade with the United States. May I point out that during the last three years we have had a larger favourable balance of trade than ever before in all the history of our dealings with the United States. Not a word from them. Not a cheer. I want to point out that in 1912, 1913 and 1914 when they were in the seats of office, not only was there an unfavourable balance of trade, but it was the largest unfavourable balance that had ever existed between Canada and the United States. I have looked through the Hansards of those years; I have gone over the remarks of some of the distinguished gentlemen who were making history at that time, and I could not find a cheep from them. There was not even a flutter of a wing. Never can you find in the records of Hansard any discussion of the balance of trade when our friends are in office, not because the balance is favourable but because when they are at the helm all is well and they do not care.
I will tell them the remedy for any unfavourable balance. If they should have the misfortune to get back to office, I can tell them how they can straighten up this balance of trade. We import from the United States a great many products, such as rubber and so on which are not produced in that country. We also import a number of raw materials for our manufactures. A few of these are manila, sisal, raw silk, bauxite, coal, crude oil, raw cotton, rubber, and so on. I have figured out the total, which by no means covers all the items, as $106,582,000. Why do we buy those materials? What a strange thing for protectionist manufacturers to do!
'Mr. Deachman.]
They buy where they can buy the cheapest, just as ordinary people do. If they want to make my hon. friends happy, they should order them in some other country and pay larger amounts for hauling a greater distance. Most of these items are free or nearly free of duty, and they represent raw materials for our industry. What matter if we have an adverse balance? As far as that is concerned, Canada is capable of paying her debts; she always has been and always will be. What does it matter whether we buy in one country or another?
I should like to quote just one more statement which shows where we are going in regard to these things. This time I quote from the London Spectator of November 25, 1938. In discussing these treaties it has this to say:
The fundamental value of the Anglo-American trade agreement lies as much in the sacrifices each country was ready to make as in the advantages it secured for its own traders- for till it is realized that every such negotiation must be based on the simple principle of give-and-take the attempt of each side to concentrate on taking must spell inevitable disaster.
That is the fundamental basis of negotiation. There must be giving and taking. If there is concentration upon the one factor of taking all for themselves, then the agreement on the day it is signed will contain in itself the seeds of decay-it will break down; it will not work out in practice. There must be a freedom and breadth of view. Alas I am sorry to say we shall not get that from my friends on the left. But we shall get it from those who are associated with me spiritually, although on the other side of the house. Then the article goes on to say:
It means that the principle of modifying the Ottawa agreements of 1932 has been conceded. Ottawa, creating the British imperial zollverein of which Joseph Chamberlain dreamed, had good effects and bad. It increased trade within the empire. It to some extent decreased the trade and to a considerable extent increased the suspicions and antagonisms of states outside the empire, particularly the United States and Germany. Since then, and to some extent in consequence, Germany has developed a closed economy based on trade by barter, which makes the prospect of any beneficial commercial agreement with her remote. But that fact, unfortunate in itself, has had some favourable reactions, in producing the recognition among states which still prefer free interchange of the need for increasing trade among themselves. The Anglo-American agreement has gone far to meet that need, for through the operation of the most-favoured-nation clause it means that the tariffs of both countries are lowered not merely in relation to one another but to all countries with which they have signed mostfavoured-nation treaties.
And finally:
In what form and by what methods the Ottawa circle can be widened, with economic

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
consequences that would produce political results no less valuable than the economic, are matters for further thought. But Mr. Hull, Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. Stanley have performed a service of no small value in turning the minds of all reflective men in that direction.
Please note that the suggestion is that it was turning the minds of reflective men to that solution of the problem.
The measure of a master is in bringing all men around to his opinion twenty years later. Well, I think if Sir Wilfrid Laurier could look down upon the scenes of to-day he would say that it was a little late. It is twenty-eight years since he made his great venture in bringing about better relations, wider trade, better feeling and a closer understanding between the two neighbouring nations. In making that estimate of twenty years Emerson, who wrote those words, was of course not familiar with the resistance of certain characteristically protectionist minds in the Dominion of Canada; but it is worth while to think that what we are doing to-day, though it may not be accepted now, will, in the fulness of time, with broader minds and deeper conceptions of human interest, bring at least even the most reactionary to a realization of the facts and enable us to establish better relations not only on this continent but throughout the entire world. And the world must be taken into consideration in the things we are doing. We shall be fair not only to those who are on this continent but to those on every continent, broadening our trade, expanding our effort, bringing about the betterment of the human race, a better standard of living and the establishment of broader conceptions in the world we are trying to build.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to follow the argument of my eloquent friend from Huron North (Mr. Deachman). We have been treated to this free trade lecture of his on so many occasions that it has become quite familiar to us.
I wish it to be clearly understood at the outset that I am not opposed to trade treaties with the United States or any other country so long as those treaties are mutually beneficial. I am thoroughly convinced that no trade treaty made with any country will have the slightest effect upon either country in case of war. Trade treaties were never consummated with the idea of making goodwill between nations. They are simply a coldblooded business proposition. Trade treaties are very often objectionable not so much in themselves as in the unjust manner in which they are too frequently administered. This particular trade treaty lends itself to just that
sort of abuse. It has as many holes in it asa sieve. I intend to deal with this trade treaty on a business basis, ignoring the assumption that it may affect in the slightest degree the relations between Great Britain or Canada and the United States.
This treaty covers so many classes of goods and such a variety of items that it is bound to have repercussions, the importance of which it is difficult to estimate until the treaty has been in operation for some time. Nevertheless it is quite apparent, upon even a casual perusal of its provisions, that Canadian industry and Canadian agriculture will be adversely affected, and that our preferences in the British market will be seriously impaired. And mark you, Mr. Speaker, it was not incumbent upon Canada to sacrifice the principles of empire economic unity to retain good relations with the United States because we already have them. To my mind this treaty displays an absurd idealism, and is the height of economic folly. It is too great a venture in altruism for a young country like Canada to take, and it was altogether unnecessary that Canada should make these concessions to retain Anglo-Saxon unity.
Let us look at a few of the provisions of the treaty. Take cattle, for example. The duty has been reduced from two cents to one and a half cents a pound, so that the average steer, weighing one thousand pounds, will now pay a duty of $15 entering the United States instead of $20. Now, $15 is a very high duty with cattle prices as they are on. both sides of the line to-day. There is also a joker in this tariff-two of them, in fact. One of them is that only 60,000 head of cattle can be sent across into the United States in any three months. We know that in Canada our cattle are largely shipped twice a year. The stall-fed cattle go out in late winter or early spring, and the grass-fed cattle go out in the fall. The other joker is that the quota of 225,000 head of cattle is not Canada's quota but the maximum number of cattle that the United States government will permit to enter their country in any one year, and we just get a share of that quota.
What has happened already this year? This treaty went into operation on the first day of January, and before the month of January was out the quota was taken up, Mexico having shipped into the United States almost as many cattle as Canada; so from February 1 to April 1, a period of two months, the duty will be doubled to three cents a pound, or $30 on the average steer, and it will be the first of April before our cattle can be shipped in again at the reduced treaty rate-

Take dairy cows and calves. The duty has been left the same, but the quota has been increased. But our quota in neither dairy cows nor calves was taken up last year; yet the treaty increases quotas which we have not been able to fill in the past.
The duties on live hogs and dressed pork are reduced to such an extent as to permit United States producers to have the trade they had in the Canadian market before these duties were imposed, and that trade was a substantial one. [DOT]
Take the duty on cream. It has been reduced from 35 cents to 28-3 cents. These fellows at Washington did some close figuring, with their 28-3 cents. That duty is just as prohibitive on a gallon of cream as a duty of 35 cents. They have also increased the quota to 1,500,000 pounds. How much did we ship last year? Only 5,096 gallons of cream; that is all. It is quite easy to raise the quota on something we are not shipping into the United States.

I shall tell the hon.
gentleman in a moment if he will just wait.
Again, take milk. The duty has been cut in two, from six and a half cents to three and a quarter cents. It may induce the exportation of more milk, but last year we sent them the bagatelle of 2,470 gallons. We are not shipping milk there, and the concession is of no consequence.
I will now come to the potatoes referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). The duty was formerly 45 cents upon exports to the United States and 75 cents upon imports into Canada. What has been done? The duty on exports to the United States has been reduced from 45 cents per 100 pounds to 374 cents-not a very material reduction. But here is the joker: it is good for only nine months. For three months- December, January and February-the exporter must pay 60 cents per 100 pounds, and those are the months when farmers who have stored their potatoes in root houses and cellars are sending them out. What has Canada done? Where is her 75 cents duty? It is gone-"gone with the wind." Potatoes come in here free with the exception of six weeks, and during those six weeks, from the middle of June to July 30, all they pay is 374 cents. In other words, for nine months Canada must pay 374 cents to get potatoes into the United States, and for the remaining three months of the year we pay 60 cents, while the Americans send in their potatoes free for ten and a half months and pay only 374 cents during the other six weeks.

I have heard a great deal in this house about the splendid men whom the government sent to Washington to make this treaty, but I venture to say they did not know potatoes. You could not have picked any three farmers out of this house-I do not care what side you picked them from-who would have signed a lopsided, jug-handled treaty of that sort.
Canada receives no concessions upon wheat, wheat flour, corn, or corn products, and malting barley retains the almost prohibitive duty of 40 cents per 100 pounds.
In this agreement the interests of Canadian manufacturers and Canadian growers of fruit and vegetables have been ignored, and our agriculture has received a staggering blow. The United States have made no concession to Canada which has cost them anything. Suppose that all the concessions they have made belonged only to Canada; suppose that Canada alone were to fill all the quotas which the United States have given-which we shall not do-it would be only a fraction of one per cent of the requirements of the United States. They have kept over 99 per cent of the market for themselves. I repeat that they have given us nothing which- has cost them anything.
On the other hand, what has Canada done? Canada has opened up her market to her principal competitor, the United States of America. She has opened it up to a country with from ten to twelve times her population, and not only to that country but to some thirty other nations which, under the favoured nation clause, will have the same concessions in the Canadian market as has the United States.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES    CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Since 1932 the United
States has looked with a great deal of envy on the preference which her competitor had in the British market. She set herself resolutely to destroy those agreements. I say that no country can prosper or give to its people permanent employment if she permits the importation of goods which she has the capacity to produce. When we send our money out of the country we never see it again. When we spend our money at home we are giving employment to our people, and we are building up markets for both industry and agriculture.
Everything which is required to satisfy the needs of humanity can be and is being produced within the confines of the far-flung British empire. Joseph Chamberlain was the first man to be seized of this great idea, and he was the first British statesman who advocated empire preferences. It is true that he went down to defeat advocating them; but his son, the present Prime Minister of Great Britain, had the honohir of signing at Ottawa in 1932 agreements containing the very provisions for which his father had met
defeat. Those provisions kept this country solvent and saved our farmers from bankruptcy. Those of us who were in the house at that time well remember how the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), then leader of the opposition, opposed these treaties, how he kept us here week after week, denouncing them, and stating that when he caine into office he would repeal them, and how he gathered into line his followers and had them vote against the treaties to a man; not quite to a man; there was one hon. member who voted with us at that time, and he will go down in history as the only Liberal in the house who had sound judgment. Yet, with all the opposition they have received, these treaties have kept this country from bankruptcy since 1932.

speechtext:
The treaties with the
United States have always been precarious affairs. Their tariffs have moved back and forth like a weaver's shuttle, and have no stability; and I am afraid we are getting into the same rut in Canada. Industry in Canada to-day is being paralyzed by constant monkeying with our tariffs. When one government gets in, down they go; when another gets in; up they go. There is no stability. Tariffs should be taken altogether out of politics. What are tariffs? Tariffs are instruments in the hands of governments whereby they can deal on equality with other countries in which climatic conditions, scales of wages and living conditions are so different that adjustment is necessary. That adjustment should have some permanence; otherwise men will refuse to put money into industry. They will not put money into industry until they have some reasonable assurance of stability.
The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), speaking on the address, said he regretted that Canada had rejected the reciprocity treaty of 1911. That treaty contained a clause whereby it could not be terminated without mutual consent, and that gave a foreign country for the first time a say in the domestic affairs of Canada. The late Champ Clark, speaking in the House of Representatives of the United States, gave utterance to the naked truth, when he said that if that treaty passed, as he expected it would, Canada would become an adjunct to the United States. The people of Canada can always look back with pride and pleasure upon having defeated that agreement.

Canada-United, Stales Trade Agreement
But what happened two -years afterwards, in 1913? There was a change of government in the United States. Woodrow Wilson placed agricultural products on the free list, and we had n very much better bargain in 1913 with the United States than was contained in the reciprocity agreement. From 1913 to 1921 agricultural products went free into the United States, but from 1921 to 1930 we lost our markets there while a Liberal government sat on the treasury benches in Canada. It was in that period that the Fordney-McCumber and Hawley-Smoot tariffs and all the other regulations were passed that shut us out of that market. What did the government of that day do? They sat idly on the treasury benches, just as they are sitting to-day, doing nothing, and their only policy was, "We must not provoke that great nation to the south of us." They saw our markets receding; they saw the European market closed, the United States market closed, and yet they sat idly by and allowed the Canadian market to become the dumping ground for the surplus products of every other nation in the world.
Prior to the war Italy, Germany and France bought millions of bushels of Canadian wheat; but the war brought home to them the lesson that they were dependent upon a foreign country for their bread and they were determined not to be caught in that condition again. Therefore they placed on foreign wheat a duty greater than the world price of wheat, until to-day they have become self-sustaining. At any rate, they are no longer a factor in the market in the purchasing of wheat. So in 1930, when the Conservative party came into office, they found the European markets closed and the United States market closed; the only market left was the British market; and they met competition there, on even terms, from their greatest competitor, the United States, a country whose crops were ripe and whose produce was ready for the market from a month to six weeks before our's was.
In the securing of the agreement's of 1932 giving us a preference in the British market there was brought about one of the greatest accomplishments in Canadian history. It must always be borne in mind that the United States is our greatest competitor. The United States has a surplus of the same articles that we export and that we are trying to sell to that country, while on the other hand Great Britain must annually buy hundreds of millions worth of foodstuffs which cannot be produced on that small island. That is where our market lies. Another fact to be borne in mind is that the British market is not a dumping ground where the surplus products

of the entire world can be disposed of. Britain has her limitations in purchasing, and every bushel of wheat that the United States sells to Great Britain is just a bushel less that Canada will be able to sell there.
Before this treaty was consummated, the leaders of industry, boards of trade, and leaders in agriculture were consulted in Great Britain and the United States. Delegates from Great Britain and the United States went to that conference, fortified by the advice and the wishes of industry, agriculture and labour in their respective countries. What about Canada? Who was consulted here? These men went to Washington to bargain with men who had agreed upon what they were going to do. Our men had asked advice of no one in Canada, and it was natural that when they came up against the shrewd bargaining power of those two great countries they had it put over them.
The Prime Minister's statement that this treaty will create closer relations with the United States and Great Britain has to my mind no foundation in fact. It is many years since there was even a ripple among these three great democracies-Great Britain, Canada and the United States-and I ask the house, since when has it become incumbent upon a country that has made a trade treaty with another country to fight for that country? We have trade treaties with Germany, Italy and Japan. Did we send our soldiers to fight for Japan in her war? No; the very idea would be repugnant to us. Yet we have trade treaties with those countries.
It is also stated by several prominent British statesmen that the imperial government would never ask Canada or any part of the empire to modify any part of those agreements. That is not the way in which Great Britain does business. When she makes a treaty she stands by it, and it is perfectly obvious that the pressure to have those treaties modified came from our great competitor, the United States.
To my mind the treaty before us is the beginning of the end of our imperial preferences. The United States will never rest content until they have completely wiped them out. The British market to-day is the only stable market there is left in the world, the only market which we should make major attempts to develop. The brevity of this treaty condemns it, in our opinion. Channels of trade cannot be altered every few years without tremendous loss to the exporters.
The other day I read a report from Washington dated November 18, 1938, stating that prior to these preferences going into

Supply-Public Works
effect in 1930 they had sold large quantities of wheat to the United Kingdom; that their trade had gone down materially, but that they expected to regain it on getting free entry. They gave these figures: In 1930 the United States sold to Great Britain 39,267,000 bushels of wheat. In 1933, one year after these preferences went into effect, this dropped to 9,000 bushels. In 1930 Canada sold to the United Kingdom 97,234.000 bushels, and in 1933 that increased to 140,459,000 bushels. In other words, prior to these treaties being signed and the preference of six cents a bushel being given to Canada, the United States were supplying 20 per cent of the requirements of the British market in wheat, and after they went into effect, this fell to [DOT]05 per cent; while in 1930 Canada was supplying 40 per cent, and after the preference this rose to 67 per cent. In the face of those figures we have this remarkable statement from two of the ministers. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other day that this 6 per cent preference was of doubtful value, and this afternoon the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) said that it was a minor factor.

Every trade treaty this government has made with the United States has been detrimental to the interests of Canada. In 1935, with all due respect to the figures given by the hon. member for Huron North, we had a favourable trade balance with the United States amounting to $57,688,000, but in 1938 we had an unfavourable trade balance of $67,981,518. That is, in three years after this treaty was signed, our trade with the United States fell off to the extent of $125,669,518, and in the same years our trade with Great Britain had risen from $191,000,000 to $225,000,000.
Another alarming feature about this agreement is that it permits some thirty-odd nations to get the same concessions in the Canadian market that the United States have been given. I want also to register my protest against treaties of such great importance being made effective without the sanction of parliament. The Prime Minister said the other day that they had authority to put this agreement into operation without presenting it to parliament. In 1932 Mr. Bennette called a special session of parliament, presented his agreements
and had them ratified by parliament before they were made operative. The agreements which were made in 1935 were put into effect on January 1, 1936, and parliament was called together a month later. The agreement of 1938 was put into operation on January 1, 1939, and parliament was called twelve days later. We are now discussing an agreement which is already law, and no hon. member had any say whatever in its provisions. The members of this house who are elected and sent here to look after the business of the country have been ignored. In such an important matter as this, even though the government may argue that they had the legal right to do it, there are things which are not expedient and should not be done.
After examining this treaty carefully I have arrived at the conclusion that Canada has been made a catspaw to pull American chestnuts out of the fire. In conclusion, because I made an agreement that I would allow the government ten minutes to-night, and I am going to do it-

It covers the office of the minister, the offices of the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister, the secretaiy and the purchasing agent of the department. What attracts the attention at once in reading this item is the substantial increase from $5,000 to $11,560 in temporary assistance. When one looks over the skeleton of these estimates, what impresses one is the almost complete absence of anything in the nature of a program for the construction of public works. The amounts are strikingly small. I think the total of these estimates is $11,000,000, the greater part of which is made up of salaries, administration and all that sort of thing. I can come to no other conclusion than that the minister and the government have in mind bringing in as supplementary estimates a very heavy program of public works. If such is not the case, why should we find in different items increases such as I have mentioned, providing for temporary assistance that cannot possibly be required for the execution of any program embodied in the main estimates? Possibly between now and the next time these estimates are up, the minister may be able to consider this matter and be in a position to make a statement to the committee. I am sure, if this is the main body of the public works program for this year, the minister must be ashamed of it. It is so trifling that it is perfectly clear that it is not the real program of the government at all. It is just a sort of smoke-screen that is put up, and there must be something else behind all these details of administration and so on, which compose the skimpiest, smallest program in the history of the department.
I should like to ask the minister when he hopes to be able to take the committee into his confidence and tell us when those supplementary estimates will be brought down. As the minister knows, it is desirable that the public works department should get its program under way as early in the season as possible. That is one reason why the estimates of this department are usually taken up early in the session, and when they are passed and approved the departmental officials prepare their program and get to work as early in the season as possible. It is difficult to get started as soon as they would like, but unless the supplementary estimates are brought down and passed by this house within a comparatively short time it will be late in the season before it will be possible to undertake this work.
Would the minister be good enough to give us some information as to why these estimates are so emaciated, so abbreviated, so very small as to hardly justify him in opening his

department at all at this stage? Apparently he is only asking for a great deal of money for salaries, because he has no program of works in these estimates. That is the very opposite to the usual procedure. The main estimates are supposed to contain the main features of the program of the government, while the supplementaries really cover things that have developed after the preparation of the main estimates. In this case the order is reversed. The main estimates which are here ought to be the supplementary estimates, and apparently the real main estimates are to be brought down some time later, possibly quite late in the session.
I should like the minister to take the committee into his confidence and let us have a statement in regard to the exceptional, extraordinary situation which is disclosed in these estimates.

I heartily welcome the suggestion of my hon. friend, who has had some experience in the matter, that I should ask for a larger amount of money for my department. I am sure that is in agreement with the view already expressed by most of the members of this house, that the Department of Public Works is not spending enough money.
The reason why the estimates are presented in this form is that we wanted to show in the main estimates what was absolutely necessary for the proper carrying on of the business of the government. That is why we have included only the items which appear in the main estimates. Another reason is that at this early hour of the session we are not in a position, as my hon. friend knows, to determine what expenditures will be required. In connection with works already begun we have not the reports of the engineers and are unable to determine, when the main estimates are brought down, what amounts of money may be required to complete those works. The reports of the engineers and architects are not all in so early in the year. That is one reason why we do not find in the main estimates what may be necessary to complete the works which have been undertaken during the year.
At the banquet which was given to my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), I think I heard someone say there was a very fine list of estimates all ready.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes; I was listening. You gentlemen were at the banquet; you may not remember, but I was sober, listening in up here. I do not remember who it was,
but somebody made that statement. Perhaps

Privilege-Mr. Pouliot
the minister could tell us something about that splendid list of estimates which were to be brought in.
Just now the minister said these estimates showed what was absolutely indispensable or absolutely necessary. In other words, the supplementary estimates he is going to bring in are not indispensable or absolutely necessary. That was the only conclusion I could reach. Of course I admit that they may be necessary for an election, but I mean necessary as public works. I should like the minister to tell us a little more about the program that is to be brought in, about which we have been hearing so much. Really members of the house should not be the last people in the country to know about these matters.
I was just proceeding with my remarks when the leader of the opposition interrupted me. I have, however, no objection to letting the item stand.
I am glad to know that the door is not yet entirely closed.

Oh, no.
Item stands.
